source.title: GSAE: Graph-Regularized Sparse Autoencoders for Robust LLM Safety Steering
source.authors: Jehyeok Yeon; Federico Cinus; Yifan Wu; Luca Luceri

record.tranche_reason: It compares steering with one selected GSAE feature against a multi-direction bank and probes harmfulness recognition alongside refusal behavior. These are conceptually related tests, but the method differs from the original difference-in-means direction and all-layer ablation.
record.gate_note: The paper cites the original single-direction study in related work, but its own relevant results concern GSAE-decoder features, a multi-direction bank, and GSAE diagnostic probes. Hyperparameter-selection values and cited results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: This is a safety-steering method paper. It learns graph-regularized SAE decoder directions, selects a bank of about 5,200 directions with a supervised probe and a judge, and applies them through a classifier gate to Llama-3-8B-base, which barely refuses unsteered (HRR 3%). Its results are its own method's performance: GSAE versus SAE and external baselines, GSAE-1D versus the full bank, and GSAE versus a safe-centroid shift. It never computes, ablates or adds the harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction. Refusal is induced on purpose in a base model. Reported HRR also mixes in fixed refusal templates returned by the input gate whenever p_harm ≥ t_hi, so HRR is not a pure steering effect. The authors say the evidence 'does not establish how refusal is implemented internally'. None of V1–V8 is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that graph regularization improves SAE-derived safety-steering directions under a matched bank and two-gate pipeline (+20.1 ∆s on JBB, +16.8 on HarmBench), with modest utility cost. They report that the procedure transfers when retrained per architecture, and that robustness holds under black-box and gray-box attacks but drops under white-box attack (HRR 51.9%). They call the refusal-trajectory diagnostic intervention-based, not a mechanistic account of refusal.
record.recipe_differences: Rather than computing a harmful-minus-harmless mean-activation direction and ablating it across all layers and positions, the study trains graph-regularized SAEs with a supervised safety probe, selects a multi-direction bank, and applies gated hidden-state steering. Its one-direction comparison uses a highest-scoring GSAE feature.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported single-direction result is weaker than the full multi-direction bank. The method's cross-model evaluation trains model-specific graphs, SAEs, banks, and gates.

fits_no_version.finding: Within the study's own SAE steering method, restricting the bank to its top feature gives ∆s 55.4 on the WJ validation split versus 90.1 for the full bank.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Probe-selected multi-direction SAE steering banks induce selective refusal in a base model better than a single selected feature.

fits_no_version.finding: No single low-frequency Laplacian eigenvector of the neuron co-activation graph cleanly separates safe from unsafe prompts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prompt harmfulness information is spread across multiple co-activation graph modes.

fits_no_version.finding: GSAE steering raises refusal-probe probability (0.06→0.72) and HRR while harm-probe retention stays at 0.87. A norm-matched safe-centroid shift drops harm-probe retention to 0.31 with HRR 57.5%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Induced refusal steering can raise refusal-trajectory signals without erasing a probed harmfulness signal, in a base model.

fits_no_version.finding: Model-specific GSAE pipelines beat SafeSwitch across four architectures and improve ∆s on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, with a small IFEval drop.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The GSAE training procedure generalizes across architectures; this is not transfer of a fixed direction.

record.problems: The one-direction result uses a GSAE-selected feature rather than the claimed difference-in-means vector, and Table 16 does not report uncertainty or utility for that ablation. The harmfulness/refusal-probe diagnostic is on a WJ validation subset and does not by itself establish separate causal mechanisms. Main utility checks concern the full system, not the single-direction intervention. The paper notes correlated judge biases; it reports a 200-response human audit but not an independent judge family.
record.rows_left_out: Hyperparameter sweeps and graph-construction or bank-scoring ablations (Appendix E.7–E.10) were omitted because they do not test the specified single direction or separately measure harmfulness and refusal. Main benchmark and jailbreak results for the full GSAE system were also omitted unless they directly bear on the versioned findings recorded here.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means direction, no directional ablation, no addition to induce refusal in an aligned model, no capability check for such an intervention.
Jailbreaks are evaluated against GSAE; there is no analysis of attacks suppressing a refusal direction and no adversarial training.
No analysis of refusal geometry (affine, cone, or multiple directions). The bank-size comparison is method performance only.
No test of whether a harmfulness representation is separate from the model's own refusal decision. The probes are applied under induced steering in a base model.
A separate pipeline is trained per model; no direction is transferred.

record.verdict_notes: Reclassified from T2 'tests' to T4. The record's V1, V4 and V5 labels are dropped. The directions are SAE features selected by probe, coherence and judge efficacy, not difference-in-means directions. The model is a base model with refusal induced by design. Reported HRR conflates steering with the input gate's fixed refusal template. The 'single direction vs bank' result compares the study's own method variants. The arXiv:2406.11717 original is cited only in related work.

versions.untested_parts: The single GSAE feature is not the specified harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction. The study does not project that direction out of every layer and position, test adding it on harmless requests, or test whether that exact intervention preserves general abilities.
No weight-edit or released-model abliteration experiment.
The attacks are evaluated against GSAE; the study does not test whether they suppress the specified direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
The study compares a single GSAE feature with a multi-direction bank and examines spectral projections, but does not test affine or cone models of refusal geometry directly.
The study uses harmfulness and refusal-trajectory probes; it does not independently intervene on or validate a harmfulness judgment mechanism distinct from refusal.

The same direction's transfer across languages or model variants is not tested. Cross-architecture experiments train a model-specific graph, SAE, bank, and gate; the instruction-tuned result does not establish transfer of the same direction.
The study does not vary when or how refusal training is conducted to test whether that creates a removable direction.

rows.subject: Llama-3-8B-base
rows.operation_detail: Steer using the single highest-scoring GSAE direction (GSAE-1D).
rows.note: The study reports this as below the full multi-direction bank's 95.8 HRR; the direction is a GSAE feature, not the claimed difference-in-means direction.
rows.check: GSAE-1D is a probe- and judge-selected SAE feature, not the difference-in-means direction. It is applied inside the gated pipeline (the input gate can return a refusal template), in a base model that does not refuse. This is the study's own method compared with itself, so it is not evidence on V1 or V4.

reader_labels.reason: GSAE retains a high harmfulness-probe value (0.87) while raising refusal-probe probability to 0.72 and HRR to 95.8%; the safe-centroid comparator reduces harmfulness recognition and has weaker refusal results. Rows r8–r16.
